The judges also suggested that the U.S. government had pressured London over the intelligence-sharing relationship should the documents be released.

The UK government has previously pressed for Mohamed’s release. Last month, U.S. President Barack Obama set a one-year deadline for the closure of Guantanamo.

Clive Stafford Smith, Mohamed’s lawyer, said in a statement on the website of the human rights group Reprieve that the U.S. and UK governments were legally obliged to investigate any allegations of torture.

Binyam Mohamed, a 30-year-old Ethiopian who previously lived in the UK, has been detained at Guantanamo Bay since September 2004, spending more than four years there. Accusations that he took part in a plan to detonate a “dirty bomb” in the United States have since been dropped.

British news organizations had challenged a previous decision preventing the release of documents connected to the torture allegations. In the ruling reported by PA, the judges said the files contained material “relevant to allegations of torture,” though they also stated that the documents did not include sensitive intelligence. Instead, they found the contents to be “politically embarrassing” and called on the new U.S. administration to adopt a different stance.

The judges further indicated that the U.S. government had put pressure on London by raising concerns about the future of intelligence cooperation if the documents were disclosed.

Speaking Wednesday to the UK’s Channel 4 News, Miliband said intelligence partnerships between countries depend on confidentiality, and that releasing the papers would have had consequences. But he denied that Washington had threatened to end cooperation.

“There has been no threat from the United States to ‘break off’ intelligence cooperation,” he said.

“In this case, the United States made clear, in documents that have been published, that there would inevitably be serious and lasting harm if that fundamental principle was breached,” Miliband added. “It is American information and it is for the Americans to decide when to publish their information.”

The British government has previously called for Mohamed to be released. The previous month, U.S. President Barack Obama had set a deadline of one year for closing the Guantanamo Bay detention facility.

Clive Stafford Smith, Mohamed’s lawyer, said in a statement posted on the Web site of the human rights organization Reprieve that both the United States and Britain have a legal duty to investigate torture allegations.

“For the foreign secretary to give in to these illegal demands by the Bush Administration is capitulation to blackmail, pure and simple,” Stafford Smith said. “It is hardly Britain’s finest hour. As the judges say, it is up to President Obama to put his money where his mouth is. He must repudiate his predecessor’s reprehensible policy.”

Earlier in the week, Miliband traveled to Washington for talks with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. After the meeting, Clinton told reporters that the U.S.-UK partnership had endured over time, saying: “Our two countries have stood side by side confronting global challenges for a very long time. We share fundamental values and important fundamental objectives.”

**UK Government, Judiciary Clash Over Withheld Torture Documents in Binyam Mohamed Case**

*London* — A widening dispute between the British government and senior judges has raised new questions about transparency, intelligence sharing and allegations of torture in the case of former Guantánamo Bay detainee Binyam Mohamed.

At the center of the clash are documents relating to Mohamed’s treatment while in U.S. custody and the alleged involvement or knowledge of British intelligence officials. Mohamed, an Ethiopian-born UK resident, has said he was tortured while detained overseas before being transferred to the U.S. military prison at Guantánamo Bay. He was released in 2009 without charge.

British courts have examined whether material held by UK authorities should be disclosed, including summaries of U.S. intelligence reports describing Mohamed’s treatment. Judges have previously indicated that some documents raised serious concerns about mistreatment and the role of UK agencies.

But the government has resisted publication of certain material, arguing that disclosure could damage national security and threaten intelligence cooperation with the United States. Officials have said Washington warned that releasing sensitive information could affect the flow of intelligence between the two allies — a relationship British ministers say is vital to preventing terrorist attacks.

The dispute has placed the executive branch and judiciary at odds over how far courts can go in making public information tied to intelligence received from an ally. Judges have expressed concern that claims of national security should not be used to conceal possible wrongdoing, particularly where allegations of torture are involved.

The case has also reignited debate over the “control principle,” the long-standing intelligence-sharing convention under which information provided by one country is not disclosed by another without permission. The government argues that breaching that principle could undermine trust among intelligence partners. Critics counter that it cannot be used to shield evidence of abuse from public scrutiny.

Human rights groups have said the withheld documents are essential to establishing accountability for Mohamed’s alleged torture and whether British officials were complicit or failed to intervene. They argue that democratic oversight requires courts and the public to know what ministers and intelligence agencies knew at the time.

The government has denied wrongdoing and has maintained that its priority is protecting national security while complying with the law. However, the judiciary’s push for disclosure has underscored the tension between secrecy and accountability in post-9/11 counterterrorism operations.

The confrontation comes amid broader scrutiny of the UK’s role in rendition, detention and interrogation practices involving foreign partners. For many observers, the Mohamed case has become a test of whether sensitive intelligence relationships can coexist with judicial independence and the rule of law.

While the courts have sought to balance security concerns against the public interest, the dispute has left one issue unresolved: whether preserving intelligence ties with Washington should outweigh disclosure of evidence linked to alleged torture.

**UK judges question secrecy in Binyam Mohamed torture case as media press for disclosure**

*LONDON, Feb. —* Two High Court judges have raised fresh concerns over the British government’s refusal to disclose material relating to the alleged torture of former Guantanamo Bay detainee Binyam Mohamed, as media organisations pressed for publication of passages they say are central to public understanding of the case.

In a series of rulings in London, Lord Justice Thomas and Mr Justice Lloyd Jones examined whether summaries of U.S. intelligence documents concerning Mohamed’s treatment while in American custody should remain secret. The case has become a test of how far British courts can go in disclosing evidence of alleged mistreatment when the material was supplied by a foreign intelligence ally.

Mohamed, an Ethiopian-born former British resident, says he was tortured and subjected to “extraordinary rendition” after his arrest in Pakistan in 2002. He was later held in Morocco, Afghanistan and the U.S. detention facility at Guantanamo Bay before being released and returned to Britain in 2009. The United States has denied authorising torture, while Britain has said it does not condone or participate in it.

The disputed passages — often described in court as seven paragraphs — summarised U.S. intelligence reporting about Mohamed’s treatment. British ministers argued that publication would damage intelligence-sharing arrangements with Washington, particularly the long-standing practice under which intelligence supplied by one country is not released without that country’s consent.

But the judges expressed unease at the implications of suppressing material that appeared to relate to alleged wrongdoing. They said the public interest in open justice was especially strong where the allegations concerned torture or cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. In earlier judgments, the court indicated that the material did not reveal operational secrets but rather described treatment already said to be known to U.S. and British officials.

News organisations, including major British newspapers and broadcasters, intervened in the case to argue for disclosure. Their lawyers said the government’s position amounted to an unjustified restraint on reporting matters of significant public interest. The media appeals placed the case at the intersection of national security, press freedom and accountability for counter-terrorism practices after the Sept. 11 attacks.

The Labour government, through then-Foreign Secretary David Miliband, maintained that the issue was not embarrassment but the protection of intelligence relations. Miliband said Britain depended on sensitive intelligence from allies to protect national security and that unilateral disclosure could make foreign partners less willing to share information in future.

The case unfolded as President Barack Obama’s administration sought to distance itself from some of the most controversial practices of the George W. Bush era. Obama had ordered the closure of CIA “black sites,” prohibited harsh interrogation methods and pledged to close Guantanamo, though that promise later proved difficult to fulfil.

Even so, in the Mohamed litigation, the U.S. government continued to resist disclosure of intelligence material supplied to Britain. That stance prompted criticism from human rights groups, which said the new administration was maintaining excessive secrecy over evidence of abuse. Supporters of the British government’s position countered that intelligence cooperation depended on strict confidentiality regardless of changes in political leadership.

The High Court’s comments added pressure on ministers already facing questions over what British intelligence agencies knew about Mohamed’s treatment and when they knew it. Mohamed’s lawyers argued that British officials were aware of his abuse and failed to intervene. The government denied complicity but acknowledged that the allegations required serious examination.

The controversy also fed a broader debate in Britain over the role of the security services in post-9/11 detention and rendition operations. Parliamentary committees, courts and rights groups have since scrutinised whether British officials benefited from intelligence obtained under coercive conditions.

For the judges, the central legal question was whether the court should defer to ministerial warnings about national security or insist on disclosure where the material bore directly on alleged torture. Their rulings signalled that claims of secrecy would face searching judicial examination, particularly when the conduct of public authorities was at issue.

The case became one of the most prominent British legal challenges arising from Guantanamo and the rendition programme. It highlighted the tension between the Obama administration’s stated commitment to transparency and its efforts to preserve intelligence secrecy, while also forcing the British government to defend the limits of public accountability in national security cases.

**Allegations: Britain withheld Guantanamo documents after U.S. intelligence threat**

**LONDON** — The British government has been accused of withholding documents relating to the treatment of a former U.K. resident held at Guantanamo Bay because the United States warned that intelligence cooperation with Britain could be curtailed if the material was made public.

The allegations center on **Binyam Mohamed**, an Ethiopian national and former British resident who was detained in Pakistan in 2002, later held in secret custody, and eventually transferred to the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Mohamed has alleged that he was tortured while in custody overseas and that British officials were aware of aspects of his mistreatment.

At the heart of the dispute were classified documents and summaries that Mohamed’s lawyers said were essential to his defense and to public understanding of what British authorities knew about his detention and interrogation.

British officials argued that publishing the material could damage national security by undermining the intelligence-sharing relationship between London and Washington — one of the closest such partnerships in the world.

But judges reviewing the case said the British government’s position appeared to rest heavily on warnings from the United States that disclosure could lead to a reduction in intelligence cooperation.

### Court dispute over secret material

The case became a major test of the balance between national security secrecy and accountability for alleged torture.

Mohamed’s legal team sought access to documents believed to describe what British intelligence officers knew about his treatment after his arrest. His lawyers argued that the information could help show that he had been abused and that evidence obtained against him was tainted.

The British government resisted full disclosure, citing the longstanding “control principle” in intelligence sharing — the understanding that classified information provided by one country cannot be released by another without permission.

Then-Foreign Secretary **David Miliband** maintained that releasing the material without U.S. consent could cause “serious harm” to Britain’s national security interests by threatening intelligence cooperation with the United States.

British courts, however, expressed concern that the government was effectively asking judges to suppress evidence of possible wrongdoing because of pressure from a foreign ally.

### U.S. warning cited

In legal proceedings, British judges referred to communications indicating that U.S. authorities had warned that intelligence sharing could be affected if the documents were disclosed.

The court’s findings suggested that the United States had made clear its opposition to publication and that British ministers relied on that position in arguing against release.

Critics said the case raised troubling questions: whether the British government had prioritized relations with Washington over transparency, and whether evidence relating to alleged torture had been kept from the public because of diplomatic pressure.

Human rights lawyers described the situation as deeply alarming, arguing that no intelligence relationship should be used to shield evidence of abuse.

### Mohamed’s allegations

Mohamed has said he was arrested in Pakistan and later transferred to Morocco, where he alleges he was brutally tortured. He has also alleged that he was held in Afghanistan before being sent to Guantanamo Bay in 2004.

His claims include allegations of severe physical abuse and interrogation methods that human rights groups say amounted to torture.

The U.S. government previously accused Mohamed of involvement in terrorist activity, but charges against him were ultimately dropped. He was released from Guantanamo and returned to the United Kingdom in 2009.

Mohamed’s supporters said his case illustrated the broader abuses of the post-September 11 detention and rendition system, under which suspects were transferred across borders and held outside ordinary legal protections.

### Britain denies wrongdoing

The British government has consistently denied that it condones torture. Officials have said British intelligence personnel are instructed not to participate in, encourage, or solicit mistreatment of detainees.

At the same time, the government has defended the need to protect sensitive intelligence relationships, arguing that intelligence from the United States has helped prevent terrorist attacks and save lives.

Ministers have said that if allies fear their classified information may be disclosed by British courts, they may become less willing to share intelligence in the future.

That argument has carried significant weight in national security cases, where judges often defer to the executive branch on the potential consequences of disclosure.

### Judges push back

The courts, however, pushed back against the idea that national security concerns could automatically override evidence related to alleged torture.

Judges noted that the material at issue did not reveal operational intelligence methods in the usual sense, but instead related to the treatment of a detainee. They also observed that some details of Mohamed’s mistreatment were already known through other proceedings and public records.

The dispute eventually led to the publication of a short summary of previously withheld information. The released material indicated that Mohamed had been subjected to treatment that U.S. authorities themselves had described in terms consistent with cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment.

For human rights advocates, the disclosure was significant not only because of what it said about Mohamed’s treatment, but because it showed that British officials had received information about his condition while he was in U.S. custody.

### Diplomatic strain

The case caused friction between Britain and the United States at a sensitive time, as both countries were trying to manage the legacy of counterterrorism policies adopted after the September 11 attacks.

The Obama administration, which inherited the case from the Bush administration, opposed disclosure of the material, while also pledging to close Guantanamo and end certain interrogation practices.

In Britain, the case intensified calls for a broader inquiry into the involvement of U.K. agencies in rendition, detention, and interrogation operations overseas.

Parliamentarians, civil liberties groups, and lawyers for former detainees argued that the public had a right to know whether British agencies were complicit in mistreatment.

### Broader implications

The Mohamed case became one of the most prominent British legal battles over secrecy, torture allegations, and intelligence sharing.

It highlighted a central dilemma for democratic governments: how to protect classified intelligence while ensuring that serious allegations of abuse are not hidden from courts or the public.

Supporters of disclosure argued that the prohibition on torture is absolute and that evidence of mistreatment cannot be suppressed merely to avoid embarrassment or diplomatic fallout.

Government lawyers countered that the issue was not embarrassment but national security, warning that damage to intelligence-sharing arrangements could have real-world consequences.

### Continuing questions

Although Mohamed was released from Guantanamo, the controversy surrounding his detention continued to reverberate for years.

His case contributed to wider scrutiny of the U.K.’s role in the CIA-led rendition and detention program, and to debates about whether existing oversight mechanisms were strong enough to hold intelligence agencies accountable.

The allegations that documents were withheld because of American pressure remain a stark example of the tensions between allied intelligence cooperation and judicial transparency.

For Mohamed’s lawyers and human rights campaigners, the case underscored a simple principle: evidence related to alleged torture should not be kept secret because an ally objects.

For British officials, it demonstrated the difficult choices governments face when national security partnerships collide with demands for accountability.

**UK and US Clash Over Binyam Mohamed Torture Documents**

A diplomatic and legal dispute over the treatment of former Guantánamo Bay detainee Binyam Mohamed has intensified after British courts considered whether to disclose classified material said to describe his alleged torture while in US custody.

Mohamed, an Ethiopian-born former UK resident, says he was tortured in Pakistan, Morocco and Afghanistan before being transferred to Guantánamo Bay, where he was held for years without trial. His lawyers have argued that documents held by the British government could support his claim that UK security officials knew about, or were involved in, his mistreatment.

The controversy has centered on a set of intelligence documents provided to Britain by the United States. Lawyers for Mohamed have sought their release, saying they contain evidence of abuse and are essential to accountability. The British government, however, resisted publication, arguing that disclosure could damage intelligence-sharing arrangements with Washington.

Foreign Secretary David Miliband defended the government’s position, saying ministers were not seeking to conceal torture but were bound by the principle that intelligence supplied by another country must not be released without that country’s consent. He warned that undermining that principle could damage Britain’s national security by making allies less willing to share sensitive intelligence.

Miliband also stressed that the UK government “does not condone torture” and said allegations of mistreatment should be investigated through proper legal channels. But he maintained that the court should consider the wider consequences of publishing material received from US agencies.

Clive Stafford Smith, the director of the legal charity Reprieve and one of Mohamed’s lawyers, strongly criticised the government’s stance. He argued that the documents should be disclosed because they relate to torture, not ordinary intelligence secrets. Stafford Smith accused officials of prioritising political embarrassment and relations with the United States over transparency and justice for a man who had suffered serious abuse.

The dispute also drew attention in Washington. Hillary Clinton, then US secretary of state, was reported to have raised concerns with Miliband about the possible release of the material. US officials feared that court-ordered disclosure of intelligence documents could set a damaging precedent and complicate cooperation between American and British security agencies.

Civil liberties groups said the case tested the willingness of both governments to confront abuses committed during the post-9/11 “war on terror.” They argued that evidence of torture should not be hidden behind claims of national security, particularly where British agencies may have had knowledge of a detainee’s mistreatment.

The case became a symbol of the broader tension between secrecy and accountability in counter-terrorism policy. For Mohamed’s supporters, the documents represented a crucial record of what happened to him. For the British and US governments, their release raised questions about trust, diplomacy and the future handling of shared intelligence.

Mohamed was eventually released from Guantánamo and returned to the United Kingdom, but the legal battle over the documents continued to fuel debate over complicity, secrecy and the limits of national security claims in cases involving alleged torture.
